gist: Data belonging to more than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security personnel was leaked online.
Hackers obtained employee records, operational names, and surveillance tools, reportedly via Okta.
The leak targets immigration enforcement staff amid growing public criticism and increased deportations.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A group calling itself the Department of Peace accessed and leaked details of over 41,000 Department of Homeland Security personnel. Distributed Denial of Secrets published the database, named Icepick. Outlets disagree on exact numbers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, citing nearly 6,600, about 6,600, 7,000, or roughly 10,000 records. While activists claim the data came via Okta, Okta denies its systems were compromised.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The breach exposes organisational charts, undercover operations, and surveillance tools used across agencies including border and immigration enforcement. It follows controversial immigration crackdowns, fatal shootings by agents, and official efforts to conceal staff identities while seeking to unmask public critics.

sections.heading: What happens next

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused executions while an independent review investigates the failed procedure.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Christa Pike survived a failed lethal injection on 30 September in Tennessee. Execution staff spent nearly an hour attempting to establish an intravenous line to administer pentobarbital. Pike spent ten days in intensive care suffering from pneumonia, severe swelling and swallowing difficulties before returning to a rehabilitation centre infirmary. She subsequently released a statement describing constant physical pain, mental anguish and isolation, whilst criticising official incompetence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Pike is believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection execution attempt. The botched procedure sparked widespread international shock. Slemmer's mother described the execution as a mess and demanded an apology, whilst the Tennessee Department of Correction defended its execution method.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review into the botched event. Lee indicated that Pike's death sentence will remain unchanged unless court rulings determine otherwise.
